547.title: Sent (Acts 13:1–3)
547.hook: while they fast and pray, Barnabas and Saul are set apart
547.howItsDone: Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday and abstain from meat on Lenten Fridays, many add small fasts of their own, and in ordination the bishop lays his hands on the one being ordained in silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rhoda at the gate, so glad she left Peter knocking. Your line was she forgot to open. What good thing did you let in? Day five hundred forty-seven.

Three verses. That's all Luke spends on the moment that starts the great journeys of Paul, the ones that carried the gospel across the Mediterranean. No vision on a road this time, no earthquake, no angel. Just a church in Antioch doing something ordinary: worshiping, and going without food. Most big turns in a life don't come with lightning either. They come on a normal week, when you happen to be paying attention.
screen: `THREE VERSES.` → `NO LIGHTNING THIS TIME.` → `AN ORDINARY WEEK IN ANTIOCH.`

segments.voice: Start with the names, because Luke bothers to list them. In the church at Antioch there are prophets and teachers: Barnabas. Simeon, who was called Niger, a Latin nickname meaning dark or black. Lucius of Cyrene, from North Africa. Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, the same Herod who killed John the Baptist. And Saul, the former persecutor. A Cypriot, likely an African or two, a man raised in a royal court, and a converted enemy. That's the leadership. Then, the setting. As they minister to the Lord and fast, the Holy Spirit speaks, paraphrased here: set apart for me Barnabas and Saul, for the work to which I have called them. Set apart. The Greek word means to mark off, to separate for a purpose. Paul later begins his letter to the Romans calling himself separated for the gospel of God, the same root. What does the church do? It doesn't send them off at once. It fasts and prays again. Then they lay their hands on the two men, and send them away. Notice that the church let go of two of its five best teachers. Sending costs something. Catholics see a pattern here that the Church still follows. Prayer and fasting come before big decisions, and the laying on of hands marks someone sent for a task, as it does in ordination today. And notice who speaks first in this story: not a committee, but the Spirit, heard by people who had made a little quiet by going without.
screen: `FIVE NAMES, MANY PLACES.` · `MINISTERING AND FASTING.` · `SET APART FOR THE WORK.` · `HANDS LAID ON, AND SENT.` · then, large: `SET APART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fast from one thing, and pray. Not food necessarily. Settle, and breathe. Pick one small thing to go without for the rest of today: the phone at meals, the second coffee, the background noise in the car. Picture the gap it leaves. That gap is what the church in Antioch made room in. Now, in the quiet you've got right here, ask yourself what you might be being set apart for. Not a mission across the sea. Maybe a person, a task, a conversation. If you pray, you can offer the small fast and simply listen. The bell holds the time.
Sent. Barnabas and Saul, set apart while the church fasted and prayed, given the laying on of hands, and let go. Today's word.
Your line: set apart. Today, go without one small thing, and use the room it makes to listen. Day five hundred forty-seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul decided to become a missionary.
what it means: a fasting, praying church hears the Spirit, and gives up two of its own teachers for the work.
what a scholar hears: the leaders' names point to Cyprus, Cyrene and Herod's court. the verb for set apart is the same root Paul uses of himself in Romans 1:1.

548.title: The Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15)
548.hook: the first council decides Gentiles need not keep the whole Law
548.carry: it hath seemed good to the holy ghost
548.howItsDone: The Catholic Church counts twenty-one ecumenical councils, from Nicaea in 325 to the Second Vatican Council, and looks to the gathering in Acts 15 as their model; bishops still meet in synods to discern together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Barnabas and Saul sent out from Antioch while the church fasted. Your line was set apart. What did you go without, and what did you hear? Day five hundred forty-eight.

Every community hits the argument sooner or later, the one that could split it in two. A family over a will. A parish over a building. For the first Christians, it came fast. Barnabas and Paul come back from their journey thrilled: Gentiles, non-Jews, are believing in great numbers. But some believers from Judea arrive in Antioch and teach that unless the Gentiles are circumcised and keep the Law of Moses, they cannot be saved. There was, the text says, no small dissension. So the church does something new. It goes to Jerusalem to decide together.
screen: `GENTILES BELIEVING IN NUMBERS.` → `MUST THEY KEEP THE WHOLE LAW?` → `NO SMALL DISSENSION.`

segments.voice: It's worth being fair to both sides. The first believers were Jews who loved the Law. It was God's gift to Israel, and the question was a real one: if Gentiles join the people of Israel's Messiah, shouldn't they join Israel's covenant in full? So the apostles and elders gather, and there is much disputing. Then Peter stands and tells how God gave the Spirit to Gentiles at Cornelius's house, making no difference between them and us. Barnabas and Paul tell the signs God did among the nations. And the crowd falls silent to listen. Finally James, the leader of the Jerusalem church, speaks. He quotes the prophet Amos about the nations seeking the Lord, and proposes a way: don't trouble the Gentiles who are turning to God. Ask them only to keep away from food offered to idols, from blood and what is strangled, and from sexual immorality. Those were matters that let Jewish and Gentile believers share a table. Then they write a letter, and one sentence in it has shaped the Church ever since. In the Douay-Rheims: "For it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us, to lay no further burden upon you than these necessary things." The Holy Ghost, and us. Not one man's ruling, and not a vote cut off from prayer, but a decision the whole gathering believed the Spirit had led. Catholics see this as the first council, the model for the councils that followed, from Nicaea to the Second Vatican Council. And notice the order: they listened first, then decided.
screen: `A REAL QUESTION ABOUT THE LAW.` · `PETER, PAUL AND BARNABAS SPEAK.` · `JAMES PROPOSES A WAY.` · `A LETTER TO THE GENTILES.` · then, large: `IT HATH SEEMED GOOD TO THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen before deciding. Settle, and breathe. Think of a decision you're facing that involves other people: at home, at work, in a group you belong to. Who hasn't been heard yet? Picture them speaking, the way the whole crowd went quiet to hear Paul and Barnabas. What might they know that you don't? Hold off on the answer for a moment. Let the question sit. If you pray, you can ask for the Holy Spirit's help before you decide. The bell holds the time.
Council. The apostles and elders gathered in Jerusalem, listening, arguing, and deciding together what seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to them. Today's word.
Your line: it hath seemed good to the holy ghost. Today, before one decision, hear one more voice. Day five hundred forty-eight.

trapdoor: what you thought: a meeting where the leaders laid down a rule.
what it means: a divided church listens to each side, then writes a decision it believes the Spirit led: no further burden than necessary.
what a scholar hears: edoxen, it seemed good, is the formula of civic decrees in Greek assemblies. Luke dresses the church's first decision in the language of a city council.

549.title: Lydia (Acts 16:11–15)
549.hook: a businesswoman in purple cloth, the first convert in Europe, opens her home
549.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Lydia, and many parishes and Catholic homes practice hospitality through welcome ministries, shared meals and hosting prayer groups; in the early Church, believers met in homes like hers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the council in Jerusalem, listening before it decided. Your line was it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost. Whose voice did you hear first? Day five hundred forty-nine.
screen: `IT HATH SEEMED GOOD TO THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Paul has just had a dream: a man of Macedonia standing and begging, come over and help us. So Paul and his companions sail across from Asia to the north of Greece, to Philippi, a Roman colony. They're expecting a man. On the Sabbath they walk out of the city gate to the riverside, where they think there's a place of prayer. And the people waiting there aren't men at all. It's a group of women. Paul sits down and starts talking with them.
screen: `COME OVER AND HELP US.` → `A RIVER OUTSIDE PHILIPPI.` → `NOT A MAN: A GROUP OF WOMEN.`

segments.voice: One of them is named Lydia. Luke tells us three things about her in one breath. She's from Thyatira, a city back across the sea in Asia, known for its dyers. She's a seller of purple, the most expensive color in the ancient world, worn by the rich and the powerful. So she's a businesswoman, likely with money, servants and a house. And she worships God: a Gentile who prays with the Jewish community. Then the line the whole story turns on, in the Douay-Rheims: "whose heart the Lord opened to attend to those things which were said by Paul." Notice who does the opening. Paul talks; the Lord opens. Lydia listens. She and her household are baptized, right there, likely in that same river. Then she does something practical. She says, in short, if you judge me faithful to the Lord, come and stay at my house. And Luke adds, she constrained us. She wouldn't take no for an answer. An opened heart becomes an opened door. Lydia is the first person in Europe whose baptism Acts records. And her house becomes the church of Philippi: after the jail scene you'll hear tomorrow, Paul goes back to Lydia's house to see the brethren before leaving town. Years later, Paul writes to the Philippians, thanking them for their partnership from the first day. That church began on a riverbank, with a woman who sold purple cloth and opened her home.
screen: `A SELLER OF PURPLE FROM THYATIRA.` · `THE LORD OPENED HER HEART.` · `BAPTIZED WITH HER HOUSEHOLD.` · `COME, STAY AT MY HOUSE.` · then, large: `AN OPENED HEART, AN OPENED DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open your home. Settle, and breathe. Picture your front door. Who has come through it lately? Who hasn't, who might be glad to? A neighbor you only wave at. A friend who's been lonely. Someone new at work or at church. It doesn't have to be dinner for twelve. Coffee counts. A seat on the porch counts. Lydia's welcome was simple and insistent. Picture inviting that one person, and meaning it. If you pray, you can ask that your heart be opened, like hers. The bell holds the time.
Lydia. The seller of purple from Thyatira, whose heart the Lord opened by a river, and who opened her house to the church. Today's word.
Your line: the lord opened her heart. Today, invite one person into your home, or at least into your day. Day five hundred forty-nine.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman who listened to a sermon.
what it means: a wealthy Gentile businesswoman's heart is opened by the Lord, and her home becomes the first church in Philippi.
what a scholar hears: Thyatira's dyers' guilds show up in inscriptions, and purple cloth was a luxury trade. Lydia may even be a name from her home region, Lydia in Asia Minor, where Thyatira stood.

550.title: Midnight in the jail (Acts 16:25–34)
550.hook: Paul and Silas sing hymns in chains, and the jailer asks what must I do
550.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Liturgy of the Hours through the day and night, singing psalms and hymns, and the Church has always counted visiting prisoners among the works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lydia, the seller of purple by the river. Your line was the lord opened her heart. Who did you invite in? Day five hundred fifty.

Still in Philippi, a few days later. A slave girl who tells fortunes earns her owners a lot of money. Paul, worn out by her following them around, casts the spirit out of her, and her owners see their profits walk away. They drag Paul and Silas to the magistrates. A crowd joins in. The two are stripped, beaten with rods, thrown into the inner prison, and their feet are fastened in the stocks. Bruised, bleeding, in the dark. Most of us would spend that night angry, or afraid, or just silent.
screen: `THE FORTUNE-TELLER'S OWNERS.` → `BEATEN WITH RODS.` → `FEET IN THE STOCKS.`

segments.voice: Here's what they do instead. In the Douay-Rheims: "And at midnight, Paul and Silas praying, praised God." The Greek says they were singing hymns, and the King James puts it as they "sang praises unto God." And then a detail Luke didn't have to include: the other prisoners were listening. Picture it. A dark cell, men in chains, and two of the newest arrivals singing. Suddenly there's an earthquake. The foundations shake, every door flies open, and everyone's chains come loose. The jailer wakes up, sees the open doors, and draws his sword to kill himself, because a jailer who lost his prisoners could pay with his life. And Paul shouts, in the King James: "Do thyself no harm: for we are all here." Nobody ran. The jailer calls for a light, rushes in trembling, falls down before them, and asks the question at the center of today: "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" Their answer is short: believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your house. That same night, the man who locked their feet in the stocks washes their wounds. Then he and his whole household are baptized. He brings them into his house, sets food before them, and rejoices. Look at the shape of it. Songs in the dark, then an open door no one walks through, then a jailer washing wounds. Years later, writing to this same church from another prison, Paul tells the Philippians to rejoice in the Lord always.
screen: `AT MIDNIGHT, PRAYING, THEY PRAISED GOD.` · `THE PRISONERS WERE LISTENING.` · `DO THYSELF NO HARM: WE ARE ALL HERE.` · `WHAT MUST I DO TO BE SAVED?` · then, large: `THE JAILER WASHES THEIR WOUNDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing in a hard place. Settle, and breathe. Think of the hardest place in your life right now, a worry, a room, a relationship. Now pick a song you know by heart. A hymn, if you have one: Amazing Grace, a Marian hymn, anything from Mass. Or any song that has carried you before. Hum a line of it, or just hear it in your head, right there in the hard place. You don't have to feel cheerful. Paul and Silas had bleeding backs. If you pray, the song can be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Midnight in the jail. Paul and Silas singing in chains, an earthquake, and a jailer who asks what must I do, then washes their wounds. Today's word.
Your line: singing at midnight. Today, when it gets hard, hum one line of a song that carries you. Day five hundred fifty.

551.title: The unknown god (Acts 17:22–31)
551.hook: in Athens Paul says in him we live and move and are
551.howItsDone: Catholic teaching, especially the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate, speaks with respect of what is true and holy in other religions, and Catholics remember Dionysius the Areopagite as a saint.

segments.voice: Yesterday, midnight in the jail at Philippi, two beaten men singing. Your line was singing at midnight. Did a song carry you somewhere hard? Day five hundred fifty-one.

Athens. Even in Paul's day it was a kind of university town, famous for its past, full of temples, statues and people arguing in the marketplace. Paul is waiting there for his friends, walking the streets, and the city's statues stir him deeply. Philosophers hear him talking about Jesus and the resurrection and say, what is this babbler trying to say? So they bring him to the Areopagus, the hill where Athens heard new ideas, and ask him to explain. And Paul does not begin by attacking anyone.
screen: `ATHENS, A CITY OF ARGUMENTS.` → `WHAT IS THIS BABBLER SAYING?` → `UP TO THE AREOPAGUS.`

segments.voice: He begins with something he saw on his walk. Men of Athens, I see you are very religious. As I passed by, I found an altar with this inscription: "To the unknown God." What you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you. That's his doorway: not their mistakes, but their own altar, their own honest admission that there was something they did not know. Then he describes God in words a Greek could follow. The God who made the world doesn't live in temples made by hands, and doesn't need anything from us, since he gives everyone life and breath. He made all nations from one, so that they would seek him, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him, though he is not far from any of us. And then the famous line, in the Douay-Rheims: "For in him we live, and move, and are." Paul even quotes their own poets: we are also his offspring. Those words come from the Greek poet Aratus, and Paul uses them to build a bridge. Only at the end does he speak of repentance, a day of judgment, and a man God raised from the dead. At the word resurrection, some laugh. Some say, we'll hear you again about this. And a few believe, including Dionysius, a member of the court, and a woman named Damaris. The Catholic Church draws on this speech when it teaches that other religions often reflect a ray of the truth, and that God is near to every person who seeks.
screen: `TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.` · `NOT FAR FROM ANY OF US.` · `IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE, AND ARE.` · `SOME LAUGH, SOME BELIEVE.` · then, large: `WE ARE ALSO HIS OFFSPRING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find God in your culture. Settle, and breathe. Think about the culture around you this week: a song stuck in your head, a show, a line in a movie, a piece of art, a sports moment. Is there an altar in it, so to speak? Some longing, some question, some reach toward something bigger, that it never quite names? Paul looked at a city full of statues and found a doorway. Look for one doorway in yours. If you pray, you can remember that in him we live, and move, and are, even here. The bell holds the time.
The unknown god. The altar Paul found in Athens, and the doorway he made of it: the God not far from any of us. Today's word.
Your line: in him we live. Today, notice one ordinary moment, a breath, a step, a meal, and remember whose world it happens in. Day five hundred fifty-one.

552.title: Tentmakers (Acts 18)
552.hook: Priscilla and Aquila work with Paul and teach Apollos more perfectly
552.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saints Aquila and Priscilla, traditionally on July 8, and the Church teaches the dignity of ordinary work; many lay Catholics serve as catechists alongside their jobs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the altar to the unknown God in Athens. Your line was in him we live. Where did you notice it? Day five hundred fifty-two.

Picture a workshop in Corinth, a busy port city. Leather and canvas, needles, awls, the smell of hides. Three people bent over their work, talking while they stitch. One of them is the Apostle Paul. We tend to imagine Paul preaching to crowds or writing letters, and he did both. But much of his week, he was working with his hands to pay his own way. Luke tells us exactly what the job was: they were tentmakers.
screen: `A WORKSHOP IN CORINTH.` → `PAUL WITH A NEEDLE.` → `THEY WERE TENTMAKERS.`

segments.voice: The other two are a married couple, Aquila and Priscilla. They're Jews who had recently come from Rome, because the emperor Claudius had ordered Jews to leave the city. Paul stays with them, the text says, because they shared his trade. He works with them through the week, and on the Sabbath he speaks in the synagogue. The Greek word is skenopoioi, tent makers, though it may have meant leatherworkers more broadly. Paul reminds the Thessalonians, in a letter probably written from Corinth, that he worked night and day so as not to be a burden to anyone. Now jump ahead. Priscilla and Aquila move with Paul to Ephesus, and a man arrives there named Apollos, from Alexandria. He's eloquent, mighty in the scriptures, on fire, teaching accurately about Jesus. But he knows only the baptism of John. So what do Priscilla and Aquila do? They don't correct him in front of everyone. In the Douay-Rheims, they "took him to them, and expounded to him the way of the Lord more diligently." The Greek means more exactly, more accurately; older English Bibles put it as more perfectly, which is today's line. They take him aside. Probably to their home, maybe their workshop. They fill in what he's missing. And then they send him on, with letters of recommendation, and Apollos becomes a great help to the believers in Achaia. Notice something else: more than once, Luke names Priscilla first. Many scholars think that means she was the better known of the two, maybe the leading teacher. A woman and her husband, two tentmakers, quietly shaped a preacher Paul later names in the same breath as himself and Peter. Catholics honor them as saints.
screen: `AQUILA AND PRISCILLA, FROM ROME.` · `PAUL WORKS WITH HIS HANDS.` · `APOLLOS, ELOQUENT, BUT MISSING SOMETHING.` · `THEY TOOK HIM ASIDE.` · then, large: `MORE PERFECTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: teach someone gently. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is good at something, enthusiastic, maybe a little ahead of what they know. A new coworker, a younger relative, a friend who's just discovered something. Is there a piece they're missing? Picture doing what Priscilla and Aquila did: not correcting them in public, not showing off, but taking them aside, adding what you know, and then cheering them on. And think of who once did that for you. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Tentmakers. Paul, Priscilla and Aquila, working with their hands, and taking a gifted preacher aside to teach him more perfectly. Today's word.
Your line: more perfectly. Today, if you need to correct someone, do it privately, kindly, and then cheer them on. Day five hundred fifty-two.

what it means: he worked with his hands alongside a married couple, who later quietly taught a famous preacher what he was missing.

553.title: Eutychus (Acts 20:7–12)
553.hook: a young man falls asleep during Paul's long sermon and falls from a window
553.howItsDone: Catholics gather on Sunday, the first day of the week, for Mass, where the homily follows the Gospel and the Eucharist follows the homily; Sunday Mass is an obligation for Catholics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tentmakers, Priscilla and Aquila, taking Apollos aside. Your line was more perfectly. Did you teach anyone gently? Day five hundred fifty-three.

If you have ever fought to stay awake through a long homily, a lecture, or a work meeting that should have been an email, this story is for you. It's in the Bible. And the long speaker isn't some dull preacher. It's the Apostle Paul. And the listener who nods off is a young man named Eutychus, sitting in an open window, three floors up. What happens next is both funny and serious.
screen: `A LONG HOMILY.` → `THE SPEAKER IS PAUL.` → `A YOUNG MAN IN A WINDOW.`

segments.voice: It's Troas, a port on the coast of what is now Turkey. Luke sets the scene carefully. In the King James: "upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread." Sunday. The church gathered for the breaking of the bread. Paul is leaving the next day, so he has a lot to say, and he keeps talking until midnight. The upper room is crowded, and there are many lamps burning, which means it's warm and close and smoky. A young man named Eutychus is sitting in the window. And the text, with a straight face, says he sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on, and fell from the third story, and was taken up dead. Everyone rushes down. Paul goes down too, throws himself on the young man, embraces him, and says: don't be troubled, his life is in him. And then the part that makes people laugh. Paul goes back upstairs, breaks the bread, eats, and keeps talking until daybreak. Even after a man fell out the window, even Paul went on. Meanwhile they bring the young man home alive, and the text says they were not a little comforted. His name, Eutychus, means fortunate. Luke may be smiling. But under the humor is one of the earliest descriptions of Christians gathering on Sunday to break bread, the meal Catholics call the Eucharist, with a long sermon attached. Some things haven't changed in two thousand years.
